title: Mole, Rat, and the River: Life Where Water Meets Land
topic: Riverbank ecology, food webs, and descriptive writing through The Wind in the Willows
lens: The Wind in the Willows by Kenneth Grahame (1908)
description: Mole scrambles up from his burrow and finds Rat waiting by the river, and the bank is alive. Follow Grahame's friends through the seasons to learn what lives at the water's edge, how food webs hold, and how careful words can hold a landscape still. Pairs with the River Ecology Field Study on a real creek. Inspired by a book in the public domain in the United States. All illustrations are original.
author: Well of Wisdom contributors

lessons.title: The edge is the richest place
lessons.summary: The strip where water meets land feeds the rest.

content.title: Mole meets the river
content.body:
Mole has spent all spring cleaning his small burrow under the field. On a bright morning he scrambles up through the tunnel, pushes past the last roots, and reaches the meadow air. Scent hits first: damp earth, then willow and river. Rat is there on the bank with a picnic basket and a little blue painted boat that has been in his family and is moored by the edge.

The bank they sit on is not a sharp line. It is a **riparian strip**, the living border where land and water meet and help each other.

- Roots of willow, alder, and sedge grip soil so banks do not crumble when the river rises
- Fallen leaves and twigs feed insects and small crustaceans that feed fish and birds
- Shade from branches cools the water, and cooler water can hold more dissolved oxygen
- A healthy bank shows layers: groundcover low, shrubs in the middle, trees above, each sheltering a different crowd

Where that strip is intact, the riverbank works like a pantry and a blanket at once.

content.alt: Watercolour of a riverbank with roots holding soil, shrubs, and willow trees shading the water
content.caption: The riparian strip: roots hold soil, leaves feed the web, shade cools the water.
content.prompt: A riverbank watercolour with roots holding soil, shrubs and willows shading the water, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: why the bank matters
content.problem: Why does a thin strip of willows and shrubs help the whole river?

steps.text: List the strip's jobs: roots hold soil so banks do not crumble.
Leaves and twigs feed insects that feed fish and birds.
Shade cools water, and cooler water holds more oxygen, so fish thrive.

content.prompt: Why does a strip of willows and shrubs help the river even though the trees are not in the water?

choices.text: Roots hold soil, leaves feed insects, shade cools water
choices.feedback: Correct. Roots steady banks, leaf litter feeds the food web, and shade keeps water cooler so it holds more oxygen.

choices.text: Trees drink all the river water so the bank stays dry
choices.feedback: Misconception: trees use some water, but they do not empty a river. The main helps are holding soil, feeding insects, and shading.

choices.text: Willows stop the river from flowing and hold it still
choices.feedback: Misconception: plants do not block flow. They steady banks and feed and shade the channel while water keeps moving.

content.explanation: A riparian strip stabilises banks, feeds the food web with leaf litter, and cools water by shading it.
hints: Think of what roots, fallen leaves, and shade each do for the bank.
Which answer names three separate helps, not one huge effect?

content.prompt: Which bank shows three layers of riparian life?

choices.text: Groundcover below, shrubs in the middle, trees above
choices.feedback: Correct. Healthy riparian strips show all three layers: low groundcover, middle shrubs, tall trees.

choices.text: Bare soil to the water with one lonely tree
choices.feedback: Misconception: one tree is not three layers. Layers need groundcover, shrubs, and trees together.

choices.text: A concrete wall straight to the water
choices.feedback: Misconception: concrete has no plant layers and gives no habitat or shade.

content.explanation: Layers are groundcover, shrubs, and trees together, each sheltering different life.
hints: How many layers did the article name?
Look for the answer that lists three levels from low to high.

lessons.title: Who lives by the water
lessons.summary: Producers, consumers, and decomposers each have a job on the bank.

content.title: Rat's picnic and Badger's larder
content.body:
Rat brings bread, cold chicken, salad, and a bottle of something bubbly for his first picnic with Mole. Badger, when you finally visit his house in the Wild Wood, keeps a deep and tidy larder. Both meals trace back to the bank and the wood, step by step.

Every riverbank bite comes from a chain.

- **Producers** make food from sunlight: willows, reeds, waterweed, and tiny algae on stones
- **Consumers** eat that food: mayfly nymphs graze algae, small fish eat nymphs, a heron eats the fish, an otter may hunt along the edge
- **Decomposers** break dead leaves, wood, and bodies into nutrients: fungi, bacteria, worms, and woodlice

A line of who eats whom is a **food chain**. When many chains share members they weave into a **food web**. If $1$ link breaks, such as no algae after shade is cleared, the mayflies fall and the fish above feel it. Take one thread away and the whole net sags. Keep the base strong and the rest can hold.

content.alt: Diagram of a food chain: algae to mayfly to small fish to heron
content.caption: One food chain on the bank: algae makes food, mayfly grazes, fish eats mayfly, heron eats fish.
content.prompt: A diagram of a food chain algae to mayfly to small fish to heron, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: build a food chain
content.problem: Make a food chain for this bank that starts with algae.

steps.text: Start with the producer that makes food from sunlight: algae.
Add a grazer: mayfly eats algae.
Add the next consumers: small fish eats mayfly, heron eats fish. That is the chain.

content.prompt: You clear the trees from a bank leaving bare soil to the water. Predict what happens to clarity after rain.

choices.text: Water becomes cloudier
Water becomes clearer

content.reveal: Water becomes cloudier because soil washes in without roots to hold it, so the disc vanishes sooner.

content.prompt: Which shows a food chain in the right order from producer to top consumer?

choices.text: Algae to mayfly to small fish to heron
choices.feedback: Correct. Energy flows from producer to consumers in order: algae makes food, mayfly eats it, fish eats mayfly, heron eats fish.

choices.text: Heron to small fish to mayfly to algae
choices.feedback: Misconception: this reverses the chain. Energy flows up from producers, not down from the top predator.

choices.text: Small fish to algae to heron to mayfly
choices.feedback: Misconception: small fish cannot come first. Start with the producer that makes food from sunlight.

content.explanation: Energy flows from producers to consumers: algae makes food, mayfly eats it, fish eats mayfly, heron eats fish.
hints: Start with the living thing that makes food from sunlight.
Ask who eats whom, then put the eaten one before the eater.

content.prompt: Which three are producers that make food from sunlight on this bank? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Willow
choices.feedback: Correct. Willow is a tree that makes food from sunlight, so it is a producer.

choices.text: Reed
choices.feedback: Correct. Reeds are plants that make food from sunlight.

choices.text: Algae on stones
choices.feedback: Correct. Algae makes food from sunlight even though it is tiny.

choices.text: Mayfly nymph
choices.feedback: Misconception: mayfly grazes algae, so it is a consumer that eats producers, not a producer.

choices.text: Heron
choices.feedback: Misconception: heron hunts fish and frogs, so it is a consumer, not a maker of food.

content.explanation: Willow, reed, and algae are producers. Mayfly and heron are consumers.
hints: Producers make food from sunlight, consumers eat, decomposers break down.
Which three make their own food from sunlight?

content.prompt: What do decomposers do in the web?

choices.text: Break dead matter into nutrients producers can reuse
choices.feedback: Correct. Decomposers return nutrients to soil and water so producers can grow again.

choices.text: Eat sunlight directly to make food
choices.feedback: Misconception: only producers make food from sunlight. Decomposers break down dead material.

choices.text: Make new sunlight for plants
choices.feedback: Misconception: sunlight comes from the sun. Decomposers recycle nutrients, not light.

content.explanation: Decomposers return nutrients to the soil and water so producers can grow again.
hints: What word means to break down dead matter?
Which group returns nutrients to soil?

lessons.title: Words that hold a landscape
lessons.summary: Grahame's sentences teach how description does its work.

content.title: How Rat describes a river
content.body:
Grahame never writes "the river was nice." He lets the river glint, slip, chatter, and keep going. When Mole first sees it, the writing slows and lets you see light on water, the push of current on the boat, and the low wash against the bank. His nouns pick the right scale. His verbs carry motion. His images let you feel a place without having visited it.

A careful river description does four things.

- It names **what is there** first: willow, bank, water, light, before it says how it felt
- It chooses strong **verbs** that carry motion: the river slides and swirls rather than just is there
- It adds one **sensory detail** at a time: the scent of damp earth, the chill of water on a paw, the rustle of reeds
- It earns a simile when the strange becomes familiar: the river winding like a lazy road

Write what you saw and heard. Let the feeling follow the facts, not lead. A reader who can picture the bank will feel why Rat loves it.

content.alt: Close view of writing desk with sentence drafts showing sight and sound details circled
content.caption: Strong description names what is there and picks one sense at a time.
content.prompt: A writing desk with sentence drafts and sight and sound details circled, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: write with senses
content.problem: Write one sentence with one sight and one sound for the bank.

steps.text: Pick a specific sight you checked: willow shadow falling on still water.
Pick a specific sound you heard: moorhen chattering among reeds.
Join them in one short sentence under 25 words.

content.prompt: Which sentence shows sensory detail doing its job?

choices.text: The bank smelled of damp earth and the water ran cool over my ankles
choices.feedback: Correct. It names two checkable senses, scent and touch temperature, so a reader can test it.

choices.text: The place was good
choices.feedback: Misconception: vague judgement gives no picture. Good does not tell what you saw or felt.

choices.text: There was water and some ground
choices.feedback: Misconception: lists items but gives no sensory detail a reader could picture.

content.explanation: It picks two checkable senses, scent and touch temperature, rather than a vague judgement.
hints: Which sentence lets you smell or hear something concrete?
Vague praise does not describe; senses do.

content.prompt: Write one sentence describing a place by a creek using one specific sight and one specific sound. Keep it under 25 words.
content.answer: Willow shadow fell on still water while a moorhen chattered among the reeds.
content.explanation: Any sentence that names one clear visual and one audible, concrete detail is good. Short is fine.
hints: Pick a specific visual you could photograph, like willow shadow on still water.
Add a sound you could record, like moorhen chatter. Keep the sentence under 25 words.

lessons.title: Listening to the river
lessons.summary: Close your eyes and the bank draws a map in sound.

content.title: What the river says when you listen
content.body:
On Grahame's river you hear before you see. The lapping around Rat's boat, the plop of a water vole, the wind stirring the willow tops. Mole, who has lived by smell underground, must learn to listen in air. Close your eyes on a bank and the river gives a map in sound.

Good listening is not just "I heard birds." It is **specific and checkable**.

- High or low, near or far, steady or sudden, each quality tells you where to look
- A continuous hiss means reeds in wind, a sharp splash means something entered water
- Distance changes volume: a coot calls loud nearby, a train sounds thin beyond the field
- Silence matters too: when wind drops, the small water sounds rise and carry

On a real visit, stand still for a count of $30$ seconds with eyes closed, then list $3$ sounds with one word for pitch and one for pattern. That list is data you can return to and compare next season.

content.alt: Moorhen among reeds with ripples and willow shadows on still water at dawn
content.caption: Listen first, then look. The river at dawn smells of damp earth and sounds of reeds.
content.prompt: A moorhen among reeds with ripples and willow shadows on still water at dawn, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: listen before you count
content.problem: You arrive at the bank. What do you do first before any tally?

steps.text: Stand still and listen for one minute. Note wind, water, birds.
Write one sentence of description using one sight and one sound.
Then start the count. Description first keeps your measures honest.

content.title: Morning on the riverbank with Mole and Rat
content.transcript:
Narrator: It is early morning on the riverbank. You hear water lapping against Rat's blue boat, reeds rustling, and a moorhen calling from the far reeds.
Rat: Now then, Mole, sit still and listen. That plop was a water vole. That hiss is wind in the willows. Can you pick the coot's call from the robin?
Mole: I hear the water every second, but the splash came just once. And the coot is louder because it is closer.
Rat: Exactly. Near sounds are loud and sharp, far sounds are thin. If you close your eyes for thirty seconds, you can count three sounds and know where each lives. Try it.
Narrator: Pause here. Close your eyes. List one steady sound, one sudden sound, and one high or low call. Write a word for where each came from.

content.prompt: What makes a sound note useful on a bank visit?

choices.text: It names pitch, pattern, and direction so another person could look in the right place
choices.feedback: Correct. Specific pitch and pattern plus direction lets someone else test your note.

choices.text: It says the place was noisy
choices.feedback: Misconception: noisy is a judgement, not a checkable detail. Name the sound and its quality.

choices.text: It lists sounds you imagined might be there
choices.feedback: Misconception: notes must record what you actually heard, not guesses.

content.explanation: Useful notes give enough detail for another person to find the source.
hints: A useful note names one specific sound and when you heard it.
Think of moorhen, reeds, wind: which names both clearly?

units.title: Seasons, care, and the Wild Wood

lessons.title: The year turns on the bank
lessons.summary: Seasons shift who is active, what grows, and where the food is.

content.title: Toad in summer, Badger in winter
content.body:
In Grahame's year, summer belongs to Toad. He roars down the road in a motorcar, all speed and shine, and forgets every plan he made last week. Winter belongs to Badger, who stays deep in his sett in the Wild Wood and receives friends by the fire. Nature keeps a similar clock, though Grahame's Toad wastes his seasons and Badger respects his.

The bank changes what you can find.

- **Spring:** fresh willow shoots, nesting birds, insects hatching as days lengthen
- **Summer:** peak activity, warm air, many young birds, insects abundant, water lowest and most used
- **Autumn:** seeds and leaf fall cloud and feed the water, berries along the edge, birds gathering
- **Winter:** growth slows, many animals shelter and move less, water colder and often clearer after rains settle

Even a small temperature shift changes who thrives, because cooler water holds more oxygen and warmer water can stress fish. Where shade keeps a stretch at $18^{\circ}C$ rather than $24^{\circ}C$, trout and mayflies have more room to breathe.

content.alt: Four small panels of the same bank in spring, summer, autumn, winter
content.caption: The same bank through the seasons: green growth, summer crowd, leaf fall, quiet winter.
content.prompt: Four panels of the same riverbank in spring summer autumn winter, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: shade and oxygen
content.problem: Why might a fish prefer a shaded stretch in summer?

steps.text: Shade keeps water cooler than sun.
Cooler water holds more dissolved oxygen.
Fish need oxygen to breathe, so the cooler shaded stretch helps.

content.prompt: Why might a fish prefer a shaded stretch in summer?

choices.text: Shade keeps water cooler so it holds more oxygen
choices.feedback: Correct. Cooler water holds more dissolved oxygen, which fish need to breathe.

choices.text: Shade makes water warmer so fish can bask
choices.feedback: Misconception: shade cools water, not warms it. Warmer water holds less oxygen.

choices.text: Fish like to sit in direct sun on hot days
choices.feedback: Misconception: direct sun warms shallow water and lowers oxygen, so fish seek cooler shaded water.

content.explanation: Cooler water holds more dissolved oxygen, which fish need to breathe.
hints: Remember the link between cool water and oxygen discussed in the article.
Which answer says cooler water can hold more of what fish breathe?

content.prompt: Select the two changes you are most likely to see on the bank in autumn. Choose exactly two.

choices.text: Leaf fall that feeds and clouds the water after rain
choices.feedback: Correct. Autumn leaf drop is a classic seasonal input to the creek.

choices.text: Fresh green shoots and new nests everywhere
choices.feedback: Misconception: fresh shoots and nesting peak in spring, not autumn.

choices.text: Seeds and berries along the edge and birds gathering
choices.feedback: Correct. Autumn brings fruits and seeds and birds gathering for movement or winter.

choices.text: Peak insect hatch and lowest water of the year
choices.feedback: Misconception: that peak and low water fits summer, not autumn.

choices.text: Deep cold, snow cover, and animals shut in setts
choices.feedback: Misconception: that is winter sheltering, not autumn activity.

content.explanation: Autumn is marked by leaf, seed, and fruit inputs and gathering, before winter slowing.
hints: Autumn brings seed drop, leaf fall, cloudier water, less insect drone.
Pick changes that belong to autumn, not summer.

lessons.title: One patch, well kept
lessons.summary: A small care plan a group can actually tend.

content.title: How Rat and Mole keep house
content.body:
Rat keeps his riverbank tidy by habit, not by campaign. A swept floor, a stocked pantry, a boat tied snug with a good knot. Badger keeps his house in the Wild Wood immaculate because he lives alone and likes order. Neither tries to fix the whole river or the whole wood. They keep one stretch well.

A class or family can do the same for a creek.

- Choose **one patch** of bank, about as long as Rat's boat plus two steps, not the whole creek
- Plant what already grows nearby, not thirsty garden favourites that need constant water
- Agree who waters, on which days, and where you wrote the plan so next term finds it in the same place
- Leave the rest alone to recover while your patch settles, and record one photo from the same spot each visit

The aim is a plan someone else could continue after you, not a grand map no one tends. Small, local, and written beats big and forgotten. Rat would approve, and Badger would keep you honest.

content.alt: Garden trowel, local seedlings, and a hand drawn care plan with who waters and when
content.caption: One small patch with local plants and a written plan someone else could continue.
content.prompt: A garden trowel with local seedlings and a hand drawn care plan, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: small plan that lasts
content.problem: Which care plan lasts: one small patch with a named waterer and written record, or the whole bank replanted at once?

steps.text: Ask: could next year's class continue it? A small written plan can be tended and handed on.
A grand replant with no plan and thirsty imports cannot be kept.
So the small patch with local plants and a named waterer lasts.

content.prompt: A shaded stretch and a sunny stretch are the same creek in summer. Where do you predict more fish shelter?

choices.text: Shaded stretch
Sunny stretch

content.reveal: Shaded stretch, because cooler water there holds more dissolved oxygen that fish need.

content.prompt: Which care plan is most likely to last beyond one term?

choices.text: One small patch with local plants, a named waterer, and a written record
choices.feedback: Correct. Small scale, local species, assigned care, and a written plan lets the next group continue.

choices.text: The entire bank replanted with garden flowers, no written plan
choices.feedback: Misconception: grand scale with thirsty non local plants and no record cannot be maintained.

choices.text: A single big planting day with no follow up watering
choices.feedback: Misconception: a one off event without aftercare wilts. Care is weekly, not once.

content.explanation: Small, local, written, and tended beats grand and abandoned.
hints: The article names a small patch with local plants, one named waterer, and a written plan as the durable choice.
Which plan lists local plants, assigned care, and a record to hand on?

content.prompt: Name one seasonal change on a creek you could observe and one question you would ask after seeing it.
content.answer: Autumn leaf fall darkened the water. Question: do more leaf eating insects appear after leaves fall?
content.explanation: Any real seasonal observation plus a question it naturally raises is good.
hints: Name one autumn input like leaf fall that clouds and feeds the water.
Turn that observation into a question about what comes next, for example insects after leaves.

lessons.title: The Wild Wood and the riverbank
lessons.summary: Two habitats side by side, each with its own crowd.

content.title: The Wild Wood is not the riverbank
content.body:
The Wild Wood in Grahame's book is not the open riverbank. The bank is light, breezy, and social. Rat rows, Mole wanders, Otter plays, and friends picnic in the open. The Wild Wood is close, shady, and old, with holes and paths that only Badger knows. Animals feel the difference in their bones. Mole is frightened when he first enters the Wood alone before Badger finds him.

Habitats differ in light, cover, and ground.

- **Riverbank:** open sky, willows and reeds, wet soil, many insects on show, sound carries across water
- **Wild Wood:** tall trees, deep shade, thick leaf litter, hollows and setts, sound muffled by trunks
- Between them is an **edge** where both sets of creatures meet and feed, richest of all for visits
- Some animals cross often: Otter moves bank to wood, Badger rarely leaves the Wood except to call on friends

Knowing which habitat you stand in helps you predict what you will find and what care it needs. Do not expect reeds in deep wood. Do not expect a Badger sett in open reeds. Match your eyes to the habitat.

content.alt: Split view: tangled Wild Wood canopy beside open sunny riverbank with reed beds
content.caption: Wild Wood shade versus open bank sun: different shelter, different crowds.
content.prompt: A split view of tangled Wild Wood canopy beside open sunny riverbank with reed beds, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: Wild Wood versus bank
content.problem: How does the Wild Wood differ from the open riverbank as habitat?

steps.text: Canopy: Wild Wood is shaded and sheltered, bank is open and sunny.
Food and cover differ, so different crowds gather: woodland insects versus water grazers.
Edge between them is richest because both sets meet.

content.title: Badger talks about winter in the sett
content.transcript:
Badger: Winter is not idle, Mole. We tidy, we store, we keep the sett dry. I line the sleeping chamber with dry leaves and keep the pantry full of roots and preserved acorns.
Mole: Do you not get hungry out there in the cold?
Badger: We move less and we eat what we stored. The wood above is quiet. On the riverbank, the wind cuts. In here, the earth holds its heat. When spring comes, Rat will find fresh shoots on the bank before we see them in the deep wood, because his place gets sun first. Every habitat has its season. Learn where you stand, then you will know what to look for.
Narrator: Badger teaches two habitats and two clocks. The open bank greens first in spring. The deep wood wakes slower. List one sign of each.

content.prompt: Which sentence correctly compares the Wild Wood and the riverbank in The Wind in the Willows?

choices.text: Wild Wood is shady and enclosed with setts; riverbank is open, light, and social near water
choices.feedback: Correct. Grahame contrasts the close, sheltering Wood where Badger lives with the open sociable bank where Rat lives.

choices.text: Both are the same open sunny place with boats and picnics
choices.feedback: Misconception: the Wood is close and shady, not open and sunny, and boats belong on the river, not the wood.

choices.text: Wild Wood is the sunny river edge and the bank is the dark forest
choices.feedback: Misconception: reversed. The bank is the sunny edge, the Wood is the dark forest inland.

content.explanation: Grahame sets the sunny, social riverbank against the enclosed, sheltered Wild Wood.
hints: The article contrasts Wild Wood shade with riverbank light and openness.
Wild Wood has Badger setts and close canopy; riverbank has Rat boating and open reeds. Which choice lists that contrast?

content.prompt: Why is the edge between wood and bank often the richest place?

choices.text: Creatures from both habitats meet and feed there, so foods overlap
choices.feedback: Correct. Edges mix species from two habitats, so food and shelter overlap.

choices.text: No animals visit an edge because it is too exposed
choices.feedback: Misconception: many animals prefer edges for cover plus open feeding. Edges are busy.

choices.text: Only one kind of plant can live on an edge
choices.feedback: Misconception: edges hold plants from both sides, so more kinds, not fewer.

content.explanation: Edges mix resources from two habitats, so more species can use them.
hints: Edges overlap two habitats, so food and shelter from both sides are available there.
Which choice says creatures from both feed there, not that none visit?

lessons.title: Reading the water
lessons.summary: Clear, cool, and moving tells you what the bank can hold.

content.title: Clear, cool, and moving
content.body:
Rat knows his river by eye: is it clear, cool, and moving just so, or is it cloudy after rain, warm in sun, and low between stones? You can learn the same reading without special gear. Three simple checks tell a lot about what the water can hold.

Learn to **read water** before you judge it.

- **Clarity:** clear water lets you see stones at knee depth; cloudy water after a storm carries soil from bare banks
- **Temperature:** cool water shaded by willows can hold more oxygen for fish than a shallow sunny pool
- **Flow and edge:** a steady glide past roots means a stable bank; a raw cut shows where soil is washing away

If you visit twice, note each check in words and a number where you can. For clarity, record the depth in centimetres where a white stone disappears, such as $30$ cm or $60$ cm. For temperature, read the thermometer at the same time of day and same spot. The numbers make the words honest, and the words make the numbers matter.

content.alt: Clarity tube and thermometer beside a creek with a data sheet for temperature and clarity
content.caption: Reading the water: air and water temperature and how far you see before the disc vanishes.
content.prompt: A clarity tube and thermometer beside a creek with a data sheet, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: temperature and clarity sheet
content.problem: You record air and water temperature and clarity on a field sheet. What tells you to look closer?

steps.text: Compare air and water temperature: a warm inflow raises water temperature.
Check clarity when the disc vanishes: cloudier after rain may mean soil washing in.
A rise in temperature or drop in clarity raises a question about shade or bank stability.

content.prompt: Which reading suggests the bank is eroding?

choices.text: Raw cut bank, cloudy water after rain, and exposed roots
choices.feedback: Correct. A raw cut plus cloudiness after rain points to soil washing in where roots no longer hold it.

choices.text: Clear water, steady glide past rooted edge, shading willows overhead
choices.feedback: Misconception: that describes a stable, shaded, healthy edge, not erosion.

choices.text: Cool temperature and good shade at midday
choices.feedback: Misconception: cool shaded water is healthy for oxygen, not a sign of erosion.

content.explanation: Erosion shows as bare cuts, exposed roots, and cloudiness after rain.
hints: Erosion exposes raw soil and roots; soil washes in after rain and clouds the water.
Clear water with steady glide and shading willows is the opposite of erosion. Which choice has raw cuts and cloudiness?

content.prompt: You lower a white marker and it vanishes at 45 cm on a clear day and at 20 cm after rain. How many centimetres clearer was the first reading than the second?
content.explanation: 45 minus 20 equals 25 cm. The drop shows soil carried in after rain.
hints: First reading 45 cm is clearer than 20 cm after rain.
Subtract the after-rain depth from the clear-day depth: 45 minus 20.

content.prompt: Select the two measures that together tell you most about what the water can hold for life. Choose two.

choices.text: Clarity depth where a white stone disappears
choices.feedback: Correct. Clarity depth shows how much soil or algae clouds the water.

choices.text: Water temperature at the same spot and time of day
choices.feedback: Correct. Temperature sets how much oxygen the water can hold.

choices.text: The colour of your boots
choices.feedback: Misconception: boot colour tells nothing about water quality.

choices.text: Number of clouds in the sky at that minute
choices.feedback: Misconception: clouds change light, but not what the creek can hold for life.

content.explanation: Clarity and temperature are the two quick checks that link most directly to habitat quality.
hints: Read at eye level, bottom of the curve; record units and tool mark.
What must you note beside the number to make it checkable?

lessons.title: From chain to web
lessons.summary: One line becomes a net that can stretch without snapping.

content.title: From one chain to a web
content.body:
A single food chain is a tidy line: algae to mayfly to small fish to heron. Real banks are messier. The same algae feeds many grazers. The same fish eats several kinds of insects. The heron eats fish and frogs. When you draw all the lines at once, you get a **food web**, a net that can stretch without snapping until too many threads are cut.

A web is healthy when it has

- Several **producers** at the base: algae, waterweed, reeds, fallen leaves
- Several **consumers** at each level: more than one insect, more than one fish, more than one bird
- **Decomposers** returning nutrients so producers can grow again after leaves fall
- Connections that cross habitats: a wood beetle falls in and feeds a fish, a fish egg feeds a bank bird

Draw your web with arrows pointing the way energy moves, such as algae $\rightarrow$ mayfly $\rightarrow$ fish $\rightarrow$ heron. Then ask: if mayflies vanished, which eaters still have another path? A web with alternate routes survives a bad week. A single chain does not.

content.alt: Web diagram of the bank: arrows from willow and algae to insects to fish to heron and back through decomposers
content.caption: A food web: many chains woven together. Take one thread away and the others sag.
content.prompt: A web diagram of the bank with arrows from willow and algae to insects to fish to heron and through decomposers, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: from chain to web
content.problem: Why can a food web survive losing one prey better than a single chain?

steps.text: A chain has one path: if the mayfly is gone, the fish has no link.
A web has many prey linked to the same predator.
So the fish can eat another insect and the heron can eat another fish.

content.prompt: Why can a food web survive the loss of one prey better than a single food chain can?

choices.text: A web has alternate routes, so a predator can eat another prey that is still there
choices.feedback: Correct. Webs give predators more than one prey at a level, so one loss still leaves food.

choices.text: A web has only one prey for each predator, so it is simpler
choices.feedback: Misconception: one prey each describes a single chain, not a web. That is fragile, not stable.

choices.text: A web needs no producers because consumers make their own food
choices.feedback: Misconception: consumers cannot make food from sunlight. Every web needs producers at the base.

content.explanation: Alternate prey paths let a web absorb one loss. A chain with one path collapses.
hints: Think of how many menu options a predator has in a web versus a single line.
Which answer gives a predator another choice if its first prey disappears?

content.prompt: Select two features that make a riverbank food web more stable than a single chain. Choose two.

choices.text: Several producers at the base, not just one
choices.feedback: Correct. More producers means more entry points for energy.

choices.text: Several different consumers at each level
choices.feedback: Correct. Multiple consumers give alternate paths if one prey dips.

choices.text: Only one prey for each predator so the line stays tidy
choices.feedback: Misconception: that is a single chain. One link fails and the line breaks.

choices.text: No decomposers, so nothing is recycled
choices.feedback: Misconception: without decomposers nutrients do not return and producers weaken.

content.explanation: Multiple producers and multiple consumers at each level create redundancy.
hints: A web holds several producers at the base, not just one thread.
Multiple consumers at each level give alternate routes around a missing prey. Which two add redundancy?

lessons.title: Measuring the riparian strip
lessons.summary: How wide is wide enough, and how much shade is enough?

content.title: How wide is healthy
content.body:
Rat would say his bank needs room. Not much, but enough for roots to grip and shade to fall. Ecologists say much the same about a **riparian buffer**, the strip of native plants that keeps a creek cool and steady. Too thin and it cannot hold soil. Too tangled with weeds and it shades nothing well.

A simple way to picture it is width and shade together.

- Measure from the water edge out $5$ metres and then $10$ metres, and note which plants live in each band
- Healthy ground has covered soil, not bare patches, and layers: groundcover then shrubs then trees with cover over $50$ percent of the channel at midday
- A shaded pool can stay several degrees cooler than a sunny one, holding more oxygen for fish
- Bare banks after clearing can lose soil at $2$ to $5$ cm a year, which clouds water and buries gravel where insects breed

You do not need to claim an exact perfect width. Record what you see and ask if the strip could shade the water at midday and hold the soil after rain. That question leads to a care plan that fits the place.

content.alt: Tape measure along a bank transect with quadrats and sketch of groundcover, shrubs, trees
content.caption: Measure the strip: tape, quadrats, and layers sketched before you count.
content.prompt: A tape measure along a bank transect with quadrats and layers of groundcover shrubs trees, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: measure the riparian strip
content.problem: Lay a tape from water edge inland. How do you record three layers?

steps.text: Mark groundcover, shrubs, and trees as you move inland and note where each starts.
Use small quadrats to estimate cover, and sketch heights.
Compare two spots: a healthy bank has all three layers in order, a bare bank does not.

content.prompt: You plan a planting with thirsty garden flowers across the whole bank and no written record. Predict if next year's class can continue it.

choices.text: They can continue it easily
They cannot

content.reveal: They cannot, because the plan is too large, needs more water, and has no record to hand on.

content.prompt: A healthy shade target is 50 percent of a 10 metre wide channel. How many metres of canopy overhang does that need?
content.explanation: 50 percent of 10 metres is 5 metres. Half the channel shaded helps keep water cooler.
hints: 50 percent of 10 m is half: how many metres is that?
Half the channel shaded helps keep water cooler for fish.

content.prompt: Which measurement best checks shade over the water at midday?

choices.text: Estimate the percent of channel covered by canopy at noon
choices.feedback: Correct. Percent cover at midday tells you if shade reaches the water when heat peaks.

choices.text: Count cars on the road near the creek
choices.feedback: Misconception: traffic does not measure canopy shade over water.

choices.text: Measure air temperature only, not the water
choices.feedback: Misconception: air alone does not show how much of the channel is actually shaded.

content.explanation: Canopy cover over the channel at midday is the direct shade check.
hints: Shade percent at midday near 50 percent keeps water cooler and oxygen higher.
Which answer asks for percent canopy cover over the channel at noon?

lessons.title: Field day companion
lessons.summary: Pair this with a real creek visit and your River Ecology Field Study course.

content.title: Two courses, one creek
content.body:
This course gave you language from Grahame. Your field study gave you sheets and numbers. Use them together on one real visit. Read the bank first with words, then measure with a sheet, so the numbers check the story you just told.

A good field visit has a simple order.

- Walk the bank and write your one sentence of description before you measure anything
- Then take the field sheet: date, air and water temperature, clarity depth where a white disc vanishes, and three rock lifts listing each kind you saw under each stone
- Add one **question** the numbers raise and one line for next time, such as to return after rain or in another season
- Leave the bank as you found it, and carry the numbers home to compare

The words make the numbers matter because you know why you looked. The numbers make the words honest because they keep your memory true. Together they build a record a next year class can use, just as Rat keeps his log of river levels by his door.

content.alt: Boots on a creek bank with field sheet, pencil, and written observation before measuring
content.caption: Two courses, one creek: write your one sentence of description before you measure.
content.prompt: Boots on a creek bank with a field sheet and pencil, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: walk then measure
content.problem: What is the best order for a creek visit after two courses?

steps.text: Describe the bank first with words: one sentence of sight and sound.
Then measure and tally: date, air and water temperature, clarity, three rock lifts.
Finish with one question the numbers raised and a line for next time.

content.prompt: On a creek visit after these two courses together, what is the best order?

choices.text: Describe the bank, then measure and tally, then note a question
choices.feedback: Correct. Description first grounds you, measures test it, a question carries learning forward.

choices.text: Guess the answers before looking, then describe to fit the guesses
choices.feedback: Misconception: guessing first biases what you see. Observe and describe before judging.

choices.text: Only measure, skip the description
choices.feedback: Misconception: numbers without a word picture lose context you need to interpret them.

content.explanation: Description first grounds observation, measures then check and extend it, the question carries the learning forward.
hints: A good visit starts with words before numbers, then ends with a question.
Which order starts with description, then measures, then a question about what the numbers mean?

content.prompt: After one rock lift on a creek visit, you saw 6 mayfly nymphs, 2 snails, and 1 small yabbie. Write one sentence that reports the tally exactly and asks one follow up question.
content.answer: Under one rock I found 6 mayfly nymphs, 2 snails, and 1 yabbie. Are there more nymphs on shaded rocks?
content.explanation: Any sentence with an exact tally plus a testable next question is good.
hints: List the counts exactly as seen: 6 mayfly nymphs, 2 snails, 1 yabbie, with the words under one rock.
Then write one question that compares places, such as shaded versus sunny rocks.

lessons.title: Your riverbank stewardship page
lessons.summary: Bring every thread together on one checkable page.

content.title: Bringing it all together
content.body:
By now you have read the bank like Rat, noted seasons like Badger, and dreamed roads like Toad but chosen to stay and tend. Mole started afraid and ended useful because he learned to notice and to help in one place. Your last job is to pull every thread together on a single page that someone else could follow.

A strong stewardship page holds four parts at once.

- A **named patch** with a one line location someone could find again, such as east bank ten steps past the willow bend
- One **food web chain** of at least three links you actually saw or that fits this bank, with arrows such as algae $\rightarrow$ mayfly $\rightarrow$ fish
- One **descriptive sentence** with a specific sight and a specific sound, under $25$ words
- A **three line care plan** that says what you will plant, where on the strip, and how you will know it is working next term

Keep each part short and checkable. If a friend can stand on your patch, read your sentence and see the same bank, and follow your plan without asking you, the page has done its work. That is stewardship, not scenery. Grahame's friends would recognise it.

content.alt: Stewardship page layout with patch name, food chain, descriptive sentence, and three line care plan
content.caption: Your riverbank stewardship page: patch, chain, sentence, and plan on one sheet.
content.prompt: A stewardship page layout with patch name, food chain sketch, sentence and care plan, soft watercolour, no text

content.title: Worked example: build the stewardship page
content.problem: Build a stewardship page for a patch you know. What four parts must it have?

steps.text: Name the patch and locate it in one line.
Sketch one correct producer to consumer chain with at least three links.
Add one descriptive sentence with a specific sight and sound, then a three line plan: what you will plant, where, and how you will know it works.

content.prompt: What makes a stewardship page actually usable next term?

choices.text: Named patch, checkable chain, one sight and sound sentence, and three line plan with how to check
choices.feedback: Correct. All four checkable parts let a new group stand, see, and continue care.

choices.text: A grand map of the whole creek with thirsty garden plants and no record of where
choices.feedback: Misconception: too big, non local, and unrecorded means no one can maintain it.

choices.text: A single photo with no words or plan
choices.feedback: Misconception: a photo alone gives no chain, no description, and no care steps to follow.

content.explanation: Checkable, small, and written wins. Next year's group must be able to find and follow it.
hints: Name a small patch, local plants, one chain, one check.
Which plan has what, where, and how you will check?

content.title: Your riverbank stewardship page
content.description: Make a one page stewardship record for a patch you know or have visited. Include: 1) patch name and one line location that a stranger could find, 2) sketch one food web chain of at least three links from producer to consumer that fits this bank with arrows showing energy flow, 3) one descriptive sentence of under 25 words with one specific sight and one specific sound, 4) a three line care plan that says what you will plant (local species), where on the buffer (distance from water), and how you will know it is working at your next visit (one measure such as shade percent, clarity depth, or photo from same spot). If you can, attach your River Ecology Field Study data.
content.rubric:
- Patch is named and located in one line a stranger could follow
- One correct producer to consumer chain with at least three links and arrows in correct direction
- One descriptive sentence with a specific sight and a specific sound under 25 words
- Three line plan: what local plant, where in metres from water, and how you will check next time with a named measure
- Page could be followed next term without asking you
